nameStory: The 'sweet' in sweet black-eyed Susan comes from its notably fragrant flowers, which have a pleasant honey-like scent that sets it apart from other black-eyed Susans. The 'black-eyed' part refers to the dark brown or purplish-brown center that contrasts beautifully with the bright yellow petals, creating the appearance of a cheerful face with dark eyes.
description: Sweet black-eyed Susan is a tall, sturdy wildflower that can reach up to 5 feet in height, making it one of the giants in the black-eyed Susan family. It produces classic daisy-like flowers with bright yellow petals surrounding dark brown centers, blooming from late summer into fall when many other flowers are fading. This native perennial forms clumps and spreads slowly, creating impressive displays of sunny yellow blooms that attract butterflies and other pollinators. Unlike some of its shorter cousins, this species has a commanding presence in the landscape.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers with dark brown centers that have a sweet, honey-like fragrance when you lean in close - this pleasant scent is the key feature that separates it from other black-eyed Susans

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and stately, reaching 4-5 feet in height with sturdy, upright stems that feel firm and substantial when gently handled

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly fuzzy or velvety to the touch, with a grayish-green appearance due to fine hairs covering the surface

idTips.label: Bloom Period
idTips.description: Flowers appear in late summer and continue into fall, often blooming when most other wildflowers are finishing their season

habitat: Sweet black-eyed Susan is quite rare in New England, typically found in cultivated gardens, naturalized areas, and occasionally escaped from cultivation in sunny, well-drained locations. It prefers full sun and thrives in prairie-like conditions with good drainage. When found wild, it's usually in disturbed soils along roadsides or in abandoned fields.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, grayish-green shoots that feel soft and velvety when touched. Plants form basal rosettes of leaves before sending up flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Tall stems develop throughout the summer, reaching their full impressive height by mid to late summer. Flower buds begin forming at stem tips in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming season with fragrant yellow flowers creating spectacular displays. Seeds develop in the dark centers as petals fade, and leaves may begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Stems die back to ground level, leaving seed heads that may persist if not removed. The plant survives underground as roots and will regrow the following spring.

funFact: Sweet black-eyed Susan is one of the few members of the black-eyed Susan family that you can actually smell - its flowers produce a delightful honey-like fragrance that's so distinctive, you can sometimes identify the plant with your eyes closed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the common black-eyed Susan, but sweet black-eyed Susan is much taller (up to 5 feet vs. 2-3 feet) and has that distinctive sweet fragrance - if you can't smell anything pleasant from the flowers, it's probably the regular black-eyed Susan.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's a New England native, sweet black-eyed Susan is actually native to the central United States and is quite rare in New England, with only 17 recorded observations. Most encounters in our region are likely to be in gardens or areas where it has escaped cultivation.
compareHints: Among its Rudbeckia relatives, sweet black-eyed Susan stands out for its impressive height and fragrant flowers. Regular black-eyed Susan is much shorter and scentless, while cutleaf coneflower has deeply divided leaves and brown-eyed Susan has much smaller flowers with proportionally longer petals. The sweet fragrance and tall stature make this species fairly easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Rudbeckia relatives, black-eyed Susan is distinguished by its rough, hairy texture and moderate size.

Among the Rudbeckia family, cutleaf coneflower is the giant with the fancy haircut - it's much taller than black-eyed Susan and has those distinctive deeply-divided leaves that no other coneflower possesses.
Among the Rudbeckia family, brown-eyed Susan stands out for its smaller flowers and brown (not black) centers.
Orange coneflower differs from black-eyed Susan by forming spreading colonies rather than individual clumps, and has slightly more orange-tinted petals.

Great coneflower's towering 8-foot height immediately distinguishes it from all other Rudbeckia species in New England - black-eyed Susan tops out around 3 feet, cutleaf coneflower reaches about 4-6 feet, and orange coneflower stays under 3 feet.
Unlike its Rudbeckia cousins, clasping coneflower has small chaffy scales (like tiny bracts) beneath its ray petals that other black-eyed Susans lack.
